indicator.subject: Mathematics
indicator.sub_strand: Data Collection, Organization, Presentation, Interpretation and Analysis
indicator.content_standard: Select, justify, and use appropriate methods of collecting data, including questionnaires, interview, observation, experiments, databases, electronic media, etc.
indicator.objective: Select a method for collecting data to answer a given question and justify the choice

skills.description: Pick questionnaire, interview, observation, experiment, database, or electronic media.
Give a reason for the choice of method.
State one weakness of a chosen method.

misconceptions: Choosing a method that cannot answer the question

questions.stem: A pupil wants to know the favourite drink of pupils in Basic 6. Which method is best?
hints: You need to ask many pupils their preference.
A questionnaire collects opinions quickly.
questions.explanation: A questionnaire is best for collecting preferences from many pupils.
questions.misconception: Choosing observation, which cannot reveal preferences.

questions.stem: A pupil wants to know how many cars pass the school gate in one hour. Which method is best?
hints: The pupil needs to watch and count.
No one needs to be asked.
questions.explanation: Observation is best for counting passing cars.
questions.misconception: Choosing a questionnaire, which cannot count cars.

questions.stem: A pupil wants to know the most common shoe size in the class. Which method is best?
hints: Pupils need to report their shoe sizes.
A questionnaire collects this information.
questions.explanation: A questionnaire is best for collecting shoe sizes.
questions.misconception: Choosing observation, which cannot determine shoe size.

questions.stem: A pupil wants to find out which of two fertilizers makes plants grow taller. Which method is best?
hints: The pupil needs to test both fertilizers.
This is a controlled test.
questions.explanation: An experiment is best to compare the effects of two fertilizers.
questions.misconception: Choosing observation only, which does not test a hypothesis.

questions.stem: A pupil wants to know the population of Ghana. Which method is best?
hints: The information already exists.
Look in official records or online.
questions.explanation: A database or electronic media is best for existing population data.
questions.misconception: Choosing a questionnaire, which would take too long.

questions.stem: A pupil wants detailed reasons why some pupils are absent from school. Which method is best?
hints: The pupil needs detailed explanations.
An interview allows follow-up questions.
questions.explanation: An interview is best for detailed reasons and follow-up questions.
questions.misconception: Choosing a questionnaire, which may not capture detailed reasons.

questions.stem: A pupil wants to compare the rainfall in two towns over six months. Which method is best?
hints: Rainfall data is recorded by weather stations.
Look in records or online.
questions.explanation: A database is best for comparing recorded rainfall data.
questions.misconception: Choosing a questionnaire, which cannot measure rainfall.

questions.stem: A pupil wants to know the average number of hours pupils in the school spend on homework each week. Which method is best?
hints: Pupils need to report their homework hours.
Many pupils can answer a questionnaire.
questions.explanation: A questionnaire is best for collecting homework hours from many pupils.
questions.misconception: Choosing observation, which cannot see homework done at home.

questions.stem: Why is a questionnaire a good method for finding out the favourite subject of pupils in a class?

criteria.description: States that a questionnaire can collect answers from many pupils quickly

hints: Think about how many pupils need to answer.
Questionnaires are fast to give out and collect.
questions.explanation: A questionnaire can reach many pupils quickly and collect their opinions.

questions.stem: Why is an experiment better than a questionnaire for testing which soap cleans better?

criteria.description: States that an experiment allows controlled testing and observation of results
Explains that opinions cannot determine cleaning power

hints: Cleaning power is tested, not asked.
Experiments use controlled conditions.
questions.explanation: An experiment tests the soaps under controlled conditions and measures results, while a questionnaire only collects opinions.
questions.misconception: Thinking soap cleaning power can be decided by asking people.

questions.stem: Why is observation better than a questionnaire for counting the number of pupils who use the library at break time?

criteria.description: States that observation directly counts the pupils
Explains that a questionnaire would not give accurate counts

hints: Counting is done by watching.
Asking pupils later may give wrong counts.
questions.explanation: Observation directly counts pupils as they enter, giving accurate data that a questionnaire could not guarantee.
questions.misconception: Thinking pupils can accurately recall how many times they visited the library.

questions.stem: A pupil wants to know the average daily temperature in Accra for a year. Why is a database better than a questionnaire?

criteria.description: States that official temperature records already exist
Explains that a questionnaire cannot measure temperature accurately

hints: Temperature is measured by instruments.
Records are kept by weather stations.
questions.explanation: Official temperature records already exist in databases and are more accurate than asking people.
questions.misconception: Thinking people can accurately report daily temperatures from memory.

questions.stem: Why is an interview better than a questionnaire when finding out why a pupil walks to school instead of taking a trotro?

criteria.description: States that an interview allows detailed answers and follow-up questions

hints: The question asks for reasons.
Interviews allow the interviewer to ask 'why' again.
questions.explanation: An interview allows the interviewer to probe deeper and get detailed reasons, which a questionnaire may not capture.
questions.misconception: Thinking a questionnaire gives more detail than an interview.

questions.stem: A pupil says: 'I will use a questionnaire to measure how much water each pupil drinks in a day.' Is this a good choice? Explain.

criteria.description: States that a questionnaire is not reliable for measuring amounts

hints: People may not remember exact amounts.
Measuring cups would give better data.
questions.explanation: A questionnaire relies on memory and may be inaccurate. Measurement with a cup would give better data.
questions.misconception: Thinking people can accurately estimate their water intake.

questions.stem: What is one weakness of a questionnaire?
options: Some pupils may not return it or may answer carelessly
hints: Think about what can go wrong when people fill in forms.
People may skip questions.
questions.explanation: A weakness of questionnaires is that respondents may return incomplete or careless answers.

questions.stem: What is one weakness of observation as a data-collection method?
options: It may be time-consuming and the observer may miss events
It always gives too much data
hints: Watching takes time.
One person cannot watch everything at once.
questions.explanation: Observation can be time-consuming and events may be missed.
questions.misconception: Thinking observation is always quick and easy.

questions.stem: What is one weakness of an interview?
options: It takes a long time and may only cover a few people
hints: Interviews are one-on-one.
They take more time than questionnaires.
questions.explanation: Interviews are time-consuming and often cover only a small sample.
questions.misconception: Thinking interviews are fast for large groups.

questions.stem: What is one weakness of using a database from the internet?
options: The data may be outdated or from an unreliable source
It cannot be accessed by teachers
It always takes too long to find
hints: Not everything online is correct or current.
Check the source and date.
questions.explanation: Online databases may contain outdated or unreliable information.
questions.misconception: Thinking all online data is accurate.

questions.stem: A pupil wants to find the average height of pupils in the class using a questionnaire. What is the main weakness?
options: Pupils may not know their exact height
hints: People often guess their height.
A tape measure gives better data.
questions.explanation: Pupils may not know their exact height, so measuring is more accurate.
questions.misconception: Thinking pupils always know their exact height.
